la:noun:aetas.html:
aetas, ātis, f.
contr. from the anteclass. aevitas from aevum, q. v.; P.; cf. Welsh oet
(
gen. plur. aetatum; but freq. also aetatium,; ; ; cf. Oud. ad ; ; ; ).
The period of life, time of life, life, age (divided, acc. to Varr. ap. , into pueritia, from birth to the 15th year; adulescentia, from that time to the 30th; juventus, to the 45th; the age of the seniores, to the 60th; and, finally, senectus, from that time till death. Others make a different division, v. prooem.; ; ; ): a primo tempore aetatis,: prima aetas,: ineuntis aetatis inscientia,; so 2, 13: flos aetatis,the bloom of life,; ; ; so, bona aetas,; and poet. in the plur.: ambo florentes aetatibus,: quamquam aetas senet, satis habeo tamen virium, ut te arā arceam, Pac. ap. ; id. ap. : mala aetas,old age,; and absol.: aetas, aevitas = senectus, old age, SI MORBVS AEVITASVE VITIVM ESCIT, Fragm. of the XII. Tab. ap. : aetate (through age) non quis obtuerier, ; ; : sed ipse morbo atque aetate confectus,: graves aetate,.—Sometimes also absol. = adulescentia, youth: fui ego illā aetate et feci illa omnia,; id. Most. 5, 2, 27: damna, dedecora aetas ipsius pertulit,: tua autem aetas (of his son),: (mulier) non formā, non aetate, non opibus maritum invenerit,: expers belli propter aetatem,: aetas consularis, the legal age for the consulship, i. e. the 43d year, : id aetatis jam sumus,we have now reached that time of life,.—
Transf.
In gen., the lifetime of man, without reference to its different stages; life, Enn. ap. : aetas acta honeste et splendide,: gerere,: tempus aetatis,: aetatem consumere in studio aliquo,: conterere in litibus,: degere omnem in tranquillitate,; cf. —In , aetas = centum annos.—
A space of time, an age, generation, time: heroicae aetates,: haec aetas,; : alia, Beier: nostrā aetate,in our times,: cum primis aetatis suae comparabatur,; : incuriosa suorum aetas,: omnia fert aetas,time,; so : crastina aetas,the morrow,. —Of the four ages of the world (the golden age, silver age, etc.), ; v. aureus, argenteus, etc.—
Abstr. pro concreto, the time or period of life, for the man himself, the age, for the men living in it (mostly poet., and in prose after the Aug. per.; cf. saeculum): sibi inimicus magis quam aetati tuae, i. e. tibi,: vae aetati tuae,: quid nos dura refugimus Aetas?: impia,: veniens,: omnis aetas currere obviam,: omnis sexus, omnis aetas,: innoxiam liberorum aetatem miserarentur, i. e. innocentes liberos,: sexum, aetatem, ordinem omnem,.—
Also of things without life, e. g. of wine, its age: bibite Falernum hoc: annorum quadraginta est. Bene, inquit, aetatem fert, it keeps well, Cic. ap. ; ; .—So of buildings: aetates aedificiorum,.—
Aetatem, a dverb. (ante-class.).
= semper, perpetuo, through the whole of life, during lifetime, continually: ut aetatem ambo nobis sint obnoxii,: at tu aegrota, si lubet, per me aetatem quidem,: Quid, malum, me aetatem censes velle id adsimularier,.—
= diu, longo tempore, an age, a long time, a long while: an abiit jam a milite? Jamdudum aetatem,: quod solis vapor aetatem non posse videtur efficere,what the heat of the sun cannot perhaps effect for years,.—
In aetate, adverb. (ante-class.).
At times, sometimes, now and then, .—
At any time, always, ever, .

la:adj:aequus.html:
aequus (aecus, Rib.; Lachm. and Munro; AIQVOS, S. C. de Bacch. 1. 26), a, um, adj.
formerly referred to ΕΙΚΩ, ἔοικα, but Pott connects it with Sanscr. ēka = one, as if properly, one and uniform; others consider it as akin to aemulor, q. v.
.
Of place, that extends or lies in a horizontal direction, plain, even, level, flat (esp. freq. in the strategic descriptions of the histt.; syn.: planus, aequalis, aequabilis, par, similis, justus): locus ad libellam aequus,level,: aequus et planus locus,: in aequum locum se demittere,: legio, quae paulo aequiore loco constiterat, : in aequum locum deducere, (cf. in Gr. εἰς τὸ ἴσοϝ καταβαίνειν, Xen. Anab. 4, 6, 18).—Trop.: sive loquitur ex inferiore loco sive aequo sive ex superiore,i. e. before the judges, sitting on raised seats, or in the Senate, or in the assembly of the people from the rostra,: meos multos et ex superiore et ex aequo loco sermones habitos cum tuā summā laude,from the tribune, and on private matters,.—In the histt., sometimes subst.: aequum, i, n., with a gen., level ground, a plain: facilem in aequo campi victoriam fore,: ut primum agmen aequo, ceteri per acclive jugum insurgerent,: in aequum digredi,: in aequo obstare,; .—Also, an eminence, if it rises without inequalities: dum Romanae cohortes in aequum eniterentur,up the slope,.—As a level place is more favorable for military operations than an uneven one, aequus has the signif.,
Favorable, convenient, advantageous (as its opp., iniquus, uneven, has that of unfavorable, etc.).
Of place: locum se aequum ad dimicandum dedisse,: etsi non aequum locum videbat suis,: non hic silvas nec paludes, sed aequis locis aequos deos,. —
Of time: judicium aequiore tempore fieri oportere, more propitious, Cic. Corn. Fragm. ap. : et tempore et loco aequo,: tempore aequo,.—
In gen., of persons or things (freq. and class.), favorable, kind, friendly, benevolent, etc.; constr. absol. with dat., or in and acc. (in poets in with abl.).
Absol.: consequeris, ut eos ipsos, quos contra statuas, aequos placatosque dimittas,: nobilitate inimica, non aequo senatu,: meis aequissimis utuntur auribus,: oculis aspicere aequis,: O dominum aequum et bonum,: boni et aequi et faciles domini,.—
With dat.: aequa Venus Teucris, Pallas iniqua fuit,; .—
With in and acc.: quis hoc statuit, quod aequum sit in Quintium, id iniquum esse in Maevium,.—
With in and abl.: victor erat quamvis, aequus in hoste fuit,.—Hence,
aequus, i, m.subst., a friend: ego ut me tibi amicissimum esse et aequi et iniqui intellegant, curabo,both friends and enemies,: aequis iniquisque persuasum erat,.
That is equal to another in any quality, equal, like; and of things divided into two equal parts, a half: aequo censu censeri,: partīs,; so ; and : aequa erit mensura sagorum,: pondera,: portio, Mach. 8, 30: aequa dementia,: aequā manu discedere,to come off with equal advantage,; so, aequo Marte pugnare,with equal success,; ; : urbs erat in summo nubibus aequa jugo,: aequum vulnus utrique tulit, (cf. : aequales urebant pectora flammae): sequiturque patrem non passibus aequis,: pars aequa mundi,: utinam esset mihi pars aequa amoris tecum, i. e. aeque vicissim amaremus,: non tertiam portionem, verum aequam,—Hence the adverbial phrases,
Ex aequo, in like manner, in an equal degree, equally ( = ἐξ ἴσου, Hdt., Dem.), : dixit et ex aequo donis formaque probata, etc.,; ; ; ; ; ; : adversarum rerum ex aequo socii sunt (Fosi Cheruscis), cum in secundis minores fuissent,—
In aequo esse or stare, to be equal: qui cogit mori nolentem, in aequo est, quique properantem impedit,: ut naturam oderint, quod infra deos sumus, quod non in aequo illis stetimus,: in aequo ponere aliquem alicui, to make equal, to put on an equality, to compare: in aequo eum (Philopoemenem) summis imperatoribus posuerunt,—
Morally.
Of persons, fair, equitable, impartial in conduct toward others (diff. from justus, just; v. aequitas, II.); constr. absol., with dat.; more rarely with gen.: praetor aequus et sapiens,; : aequissimus aestimator et judex,: praebere se aequum alicui,: absentium aequi, praesentibus mobiles,benevolent toward,.—
Of things, fair, right, equitable, reasonable: ITA. SENATVS. AIQVOM. CENSVIT., S. C. de Bach. 1. 26: et aecum et rectum est, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 81 Rib.): aequa et honesta postulatio,: quod justum est et aequum, servis praestate,just and fair,: postulo primum id, quod aequissimum est, ut, etc.,: aequa lex et omnibus utilis,: aequissimis legibus monere,: aequae conditiones,; see Fischer, Gr. II. 611.—Hence,
ae-quum, i, n.subst., what is fair, equitable, or just; fairness, equity, or justice, etc.: jus atque aequum, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 224 Vahl.): utilitas justi prope mater et aequi,: aequi studium,.—Often with comparatives, more than is right, proper, reasonable: lamentari amplius aequo,: injurias gravius aequo habere,to feel too deeply,: potus largius aequo,.—Hence, aequum est, it is reasonable, proper, right, etc.; constr. with acc. and inf., in good prose also with dat. pers. and ut, Rudd. II. p. 235, n. 21: nos quiescere aequom est, Enn. ap. P. (Trag. v. 199 Vahl.): quae liberum scire aequom est adulescentem,: significant Imbecillorum esse aecum misererier omnīs,: non est aequum nos derelinquere verbum Dei,: aequius est mori quam auctoritatem imperii foedare,: ut peritis? Ut piscatorem aequomst (sc. perire), fame sitique speque,; so, sicut aequum est homini de potestate deorum timide et pauca dicamus,.—In Plaut., with abl.: plus vidissem quam med atque illo aequom foret,would be becoming in me and him,; .—
Aequum as subst. very freq. with bonum = aequitas, equitable conduct toward others, fairness, equity, etc.: neque quidquam queo aequi bonique ab eo impetrare,what is right and just,: cum de jure civili, cum de aequo et bono disputaretur,: ex aequo et bono, non ex callido versutoque jure rem judicari oportere,: fit reus magis ex aequo bonoque quam ex jure gentium,in accordance with justice and equity,.— Also without et: illi dolum malum, illi fidem bonam, illi aequum bonum tradiderunt,.—So also, aequius melius, according to greater equily, ; .—
Of a state of mind, even, unruffled, calm, composed, tranquil, patient, enduring (cf. aequitas, II. B.); esp. freq. with animus or mens: animus aequos optumum est aerumnae condimentum,: concedo et quod animus aequus est et quia necesse est,: quodadest memento Componere aequus,: tentantem majora, fere praesentibus aequum,; and so, aequam memento rebus in arduis Servare mentem, etc.,.—Esp. freq. in the adv. abl.: aequo (aequiore, aequissimo) animo, with even mind, with equanimity, patiently, calmly, quietly, with forbearance: ego, nisi Bibulus adniteretur de triumpho, aequo animo essem, nunc vero αἰσχρὸν σιωπᾶν, : carere aequo animo aliquā re,: ferre aliquid,; : accipere,: tolerare,: quo aequiore animo Germanicus celerem successionem operiretur,: testem se in judiciis interrogari aequissimo animo patiebatur,.—In eccl. Lat. = bono animo: aequo animo esto,be of good cheer,: aequo animo (aliquis) est? Psallat,.—Hence: aequi bonique facere aliquid, to regard as fair and reasonable (prop., a gen. of value, Roby, § 1191), to put up with, be content with, submit to, acquiesce in, etc.: istuc aequi bonique facio,: tranquillissimus animus meus totum istuc aequi boni

facit, ; : aequi istuc faciam,it will be all the same to me,.—So also: aequi bonique dicere,to propose any thing reasonable,.—Hence, aequē, adv., in like manner, equally, just as = ex aequo, pariter, Gr. ἴσως, όμοιως (indicating the entire equality of two objects compared, while similiter denotes only likeness): eā (benevolentiā) non pariter omnes egemus ... honore et gloriā fortasse non aeque omnes egent,: non possum ego non aut proxime atque ille aut etiam aeque laborare,: universa aeque eveniunt justo et impio,.

In the comic poets with cum or the comp. abl. (cf. adaeque); in Cic. and good class. authors gen. with et, atque, ac, ac si; less class. with quam, ut, quam ut; in Petr. with tamquam.
Aeque—cum: animum advorte, ut aeque mecum haec scias,, : novi aeque omnia tecum, Ter Phorm. 5, 9, 43. But in , tecum una postea aeque pocla potitet, una belongs with tecum to potitet, and aeque is put absol. (sc. ut tu).—
Aeque with comp. abl.: nullus est hoc meticulosus aeque,as this person,: qui me in terrā aeque fortunatus erit,.—
Aeque—et or aeque— que (as in Gr. ἴσον καί, ἴσα καί, Soph. Oed. Tyr. 611; Thuc. 3, 14). nisi aeque amicos et nosmet ipsos diligamus,equally as ourselves,. versūs aeque prima et media et extrema pars attenditur, ; ; so ; , : quod Aeque neglectum pueris senibusque nocebit,.—
Aeque—atque, —ac, —ac si, as ... as; as much as, as: vide ne, quem tu esse hebetem deputes aeque ac pecus, is, etc., Att. ap. : pumex non aeque aridus atque hic est senex, Plaut Aul. 2, 4, 18; ; : nisi haberes, qui illis aeque ac tu ipse gauderet,: sed me colit et observat aeque atque patronum suum,; ; so ; ; ; ; : aeque ac si. with the subj., just as if. altogether as if: Egnatii absentis rem ut tueare, aeque a te peto ac si mea negotia essent,; Auct Her 2, 13, 19: quo factum est, ut jumenta aeque nitida ex castellis educeret ac si in campestribus ea locis habuisset, Nep . 6; ; —(ε) Aeque— quam (only in Plaut. and prose writers from the Aug. per.; neither in Cic. nor in Cæs.),as ... as, in the same manner as, as well ... as, like,; nullum esse agrum aeque feracem quam hic est,: nihil aeque eos terruit quam robur et color imperatoris, ; 5, 6, 11; so 5, 3, 4; 31, 1, 3; in navibus posita aeque quam in aedificiis,; so 2, 70, 72, § 180; ; ; ; ; —(ζ) Aeque—ut, a rare combination, and unworthy of imitation (in authors of the class. per. its reception rests, for the most part, upon false readings for aeque et or aeque ac), as much as, like, cui nihil aeque in causis agendis ut brevitas placet, Keil. accinctus aeque ut discinctus, . Possidebitis eam (terram) singuli aeque ut frater suus, : idemque proficeret aeque ut rosaceum,, where Jan reads proficeret quod rosaceum.—In Plaut. once aeque—quasi for the class. aeque ac. quem videam aeque esse maestum quasi dies si dicta sit, Fleck.—(η) Sometimes aeque—aeque, as well as, as much as. aeque pauperibus prodest, locupletibus aeque, : aeque discordiam praepositorum, aeque concordiam subjectis exitiosam,.—
The comparison is often to be supplied from the whole sentence or context; hence, aeque stands absol. for aeque ac, etc. (ante-class. freq.; also in Cic. and Liv.), equally, as much as, as: eadem oratio non aeque valet, Enn. ap. (from Eurip. Hec. 295: λόγος ... οὐ ταὐτὸν σθένει): satin habes, si feminarum nullast quam aeque diligam?: Aetna mons non aeque altus, ; ; , etc.; ; ; so ; : aeque sons,; so 29, 19, 4 al.: aeque non est dubium,it is as little doubtful,.—
With omnes, uterque, and definite numerals, to indicate that a thing applies equally to all the objects designated, equally: non omnia eadem aeque omnibus suavia esse scito,; ; so ; : etsi utrique nostrum prope aeque gratae erant (litterae),; so ; ; ; : aeque ambo pares,: duae trabes aeque longae,; . —
Sometimes absol., with several substantives, alike, equally: Tragici et comici Numquam aeque sunt meditati,. imperium bonus ignavus aeque sibi exoptant, .—
In , nec est mihi quisquam, melius aeque cui velim, melius velle is, perhaps, to be taken together as a phrase, and the comp. considered as used in a restricted sense, as in melius est. Others consider the comp. as used for the simple positive; cf. adaeque.—
Justly, with equity: mihi id aeque factum arbitror, dub. (Ritschl: jureque id factum arbitror).— Comp.: ferro quam fame aequius perituros, more willingly, Fragm.—Sup.: aequissime jus dicere,: judicas ut qui aequissime,, Ep. 11.!*? An old adverb. form, aequĭter, also occurs: praeda per participes aequiter partita est, Liv. Andr. ap. ; so Pac. ib., Att. ib., and Plaut. acc. to P.

la:adv:aeque.gloss: equally, as, just as, in like manner
senses: equally, as, just as, in like manner

la:noun:aegritudo.html:
aegrĭtūdo, ĭnis, f.
aeger
,
illness, sickness (both of body and mind; while aegrotatio denotes only physical disease).
Lit., of the body of men and brutes (only after the Aug. per.): visi sunt (elephanti) fessi aegritudine,: metu et aegritudine fessus,; so ; ; ; — Also of plants: sunt enim quaedam aegritudines (ficorum) et locorum,.—Far oftener,
Of mind, grief, sorrow, care, etc. (class.; freq. in the Ciceronian philos.), Pac. ap. ; : aegritudo animam adimit,; so ; ; ; ; : praeclare nostri, ut alia multa, molestiam, sollicitudinem, angorem propter similitudinem corporum aegrorum, aegritudinem nominaverunt; and soon after: ut aegrotatio in corpore, sic aegritudo in animo,; so ; 9; 12; 13; 14; 26; 4, 7; 15; al.; .—In the plur., ; ; ; .

la:verb:aegroto.html:
aegrōto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.
aegrotus
,
to be ill, sick.
Lit., of men and brutes: vehementer diuque,: gravissime aegrotans,: graviter,: leviter,: periculose,: aegrotavit usque ad mortem,: aegrotare timenti,: morbo,: aegrotare coepit,: quia armentum aegrotet in agris,.—Of plants: (vites) aegrotant,: aegrotant poma ipsa per se sine arbore,.—
Fig.
Of the mind: ea res, ex qua animus aegrotat,: aegrotare animi vitio,.—
Of other abstr. things, to languish, etc. (cf. jaceo): in te aegrotant artes,; : languent officia, atque aegrotat fama vacillans, duties are neglected, reputation sickens and staggers, * .

la:adj:aegrotus.html:
aegrōtus, a, um, adj.
aeger
,
ill, sick, diseased (in Cic. rare).
Prop., of the body: facile omnes, cum valemus, recta consilia aegrotis damus,: aegroto, dum anima est, spes esse dicitur,; : cum te aegrotum non videam, Esdr. 2, 2; : corpus,: leo, al.—
Trop., of the mind: omnibus amicis morbum inicies gravem, ita ut te videre audireque aegroti sient,sick of seeing and hearing you, (for the constr. of the inf. here, v. Roby, II. § 1360 sq.): animus, Att. ap. ; ; ; .—So of the state: hoc remedium est aegrotae et prope desperatae rei publicae,.

senses: to "build" a life, to live in a morally good or prudent manner
la:verb:aedifico.html:
aedĭfĭco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
aedesfacio
, lit.
to erect a building, to build; and in gen., to build, raise, erect, or establish any thing.
Lit.: aedificare cum sit proprie aedem facere, ponitur tamen καταχρηστικῶς in omni genere constructionis, Müll.; hence in the first signif. for the most part
Absol.: aedificare diu cogitare oportet,: ecce aedificat,: ad quem (usum) accommodanda est aedificandi descriptio,; : tribus locis aedifico, reliqua reconcinno,: lautius, id Leg. 2, 1, 3: belle,: accuratius ad frigora atque aestus vitandos,: diruit, aedificat, mutat quadrata rotundis,; so .—
With object: domum,; so : casas,.—
In gen., to build, construct, etc.: navim, piscinas, : navem,: urbem,; so : oppida, Para. 26, 6: turrim,: murum, Para. 33, 14: porticum,: hortos,: equum,: mundum,: tot adhuc compagibus altum aedificat caput,i.e. makes it, by bands and hair ornaments, a high tower,.—
Fig., to build up, establish: rem publicam,.—And (eccl.) in a religious sense, to build up, instruct, edify.
Absol.: caritas aedificat,: non omnia aedificant,.—
With object: semetipsum,: alterutrum,.

la:verb:aequo.gloss: to equalize, make equal to something else, equate
senses: to equalize, make equal to something else, equate
to compare; to place on equal footing with
to make fair or right; divide equally, apportion fairly or reasonably
la:verb:aequo.html:
aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.
aequus
.
Act., to make one thing equal to another; constr. with cum and (in gen. in the histt.) with dat., and with cop. conj. (cf. adaequo).
With cum: inventum est temperamentum, quo tenuiores cum principibus aequari se putarent,: cum suas quisque opes cum potentissimis aequari videat,: numerum (corporum) cum navibus,.—
With dat.: Insedabiliter sitis arida, corpora mersans, Aequabat multum parvis umoribus imbrem,an unquenchable, burning thirst ... made the most copious stream seem to them as only a few drops,: per somnum vinumque dies noctibus aequare,: aequavit togatus armati gloriam collegae,: cujus magnitudini semper animum aequavit, (but in , facta dictis aequando, dictis is abl.; v Weissenb. ad h. l.); ; aequare solo templum,to level with the ground,; so domum,, and Aur. Vict. Vir. lllustr. 17. 5; and in an extended sense: Scipio Numantiam excisam aequavit solo,.—Hence, trop.: solo aequandae sunt dictaturae consulatusque, entirely abolished, Liv 6, 18.—
With cop. conj.: Curios aequare Fabriciosque,. —Poet.: si protinus illum Aequāsset nocti ludum,had played through the whole night,.—Hence also,
In comparison, to place a thing on an equality with, to compare.; in Cic. with cum; later with dat.: aequare et conferre scelera alicujus cum aliis,: ne aequaveritis Hannibali Philippum, ne Carthaginiensibus Macedonas: Pyrrho certe aequabitis,: Deum homini non aequabo,: quis in nubibus aequabitur Domino,.—
Of places, to make level, even, or smooth: aequata agri planities,; and trop.: aequato discrimine,at an equal distance,: aequato omnium periculo,: aequato Marte,: aequato jure omnium,.—Poet.: ibant aequati numero,

divided into equal parts, : foedera regum Vel Gabiis vel cum rigidis aequata Sabinis, i. e. aequis legibus icta,; cf.: si foedus est, si societas aequatio juris est ... cur non omnia aequantur?placed in the same circumstances?.—

T. t.
Aequare frontem, milit. t., to make an equal front, : aequatis frontibus,; v. frons.—
Aequare sortes, to see that the lots are equal in number to those who draw, of the same material, and each with a different name. The classical passage for this phrase is : conicite sortes: uxor, aequa (sc. eas); v. the preceding verses. So Orell.: dum sitella defertur, dum aequantur sortes, dum sortitio fit, etc.—
Neutr. or act., to become equal to one, to equal, come up to, attain to (mostly in the histt.); constr. with dat., but oftener with acc. (cf. adaequo and aequipero, and Zumpt, § 389, 1): qui jam illis fere aequārunt,; : ea arte aequāsset superiores reges, ni, etc.,; so, cursu equum,; for which Curtius: cursum alicujus, 4, 1: gloriam alicujus,: eam picturam imitati sunt multi, aequavit nemo,; .—Poet.: sagitta aequans ventos, like the winds in swiftness, : valet nondum munia comparis Aequare (juvenca),i. e. cannot yet draw even with her mate,.

la:adj:aeger.html:
aeger, gra, grum, adj.
Curtius proposes to connect it with ἐπ-είγω, to press, drive; αἰγίς, storm-wind; αἶγες, waves; and Sanscr. egāmi, to tremble; trembling, shaking, being a common symptom of illness
, designates indisposition, as well of mind as of body (while aegrotus is generally used only of physical disease; class.; in Cic. far more frequent than aegrotus; Celsus uses only aeger, never aegrotus).
Lit., of the body, ill, sick, unwell, diseased, suffering.
Of men: homines aegri morbo gravi,: graviter aegrum fuisse,; : infirma atque aegra valetudo,: aegro corpore esse,: ex vulnere,: vulneribus,: pedibus,; so ; ; Wernsd. Poët. L. Min. 6, 197, 8: stomachus,: anhelitus,shortness of breath,.—At a later period constr. with gen. or acc.: Psyche aegra corporis, animi saucia, Oud. la:noun:aestimatio.html:
aestĭmātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
The estimating a thing according to its extrinsic (money) value, valuation, appraisement: in censu habendo potestas omnis aestimationis habendae censori permittitur,: aestimatio frumenti, the determination of the prœtor (legate or quœstor), how much ready money one should pay, instead of the corn which he was to furnish, : erat Athenis reo damnato, si fraus non capitalis esset, quasi poenae aestimatio,i. e. a commutation of corporal punishment for a fine,.—So esp. litis or litium aestimatio, in Roman civil law, an estimating, valuation of the contested matter; in criminal law also, the stating how much the convicted person had to pay, an assessment of damages, ; (cf. lis aestimata, ): lex de multarum aestimatione,.— After the civil war, Cæsar, in order to enable debtors to cancel the demands against them, decreed an aestimatio possessionum, i. e. an estimation or appraisement of real estate, according to the value which it had before the war, and compelled the creditors to take this in payment instead of money; they were also obliged to deduct from the sum demanded any interest that had been paid; v. ; and . Hence, in aestimationem accipere, to accept or agree to such a valuation, or payment by real estate at a high price: a Marco Laberio C. Albinius praedia in aestimationem accepit,.—And meton., with an allusion to the law of Cæsar: aestimationes

= praedia, the real estate received in payment: quando aestimationes tuas vendere non potes,. Since the creditor was a loser by this regulation, aestimationem accipere, to suffer injury or loss, .—

Trop.
A valuation, i. e. an estimation of a thing according to its intrinsic worth (while existimatio denotes the consideration, regard due to an object on account of its nominal value): bonum hoc est quidem plurimi aestimandum, sed ea aestimatio genere valet, non magnitudine,; so 3, 13, 44; 3, 6: semper aestimationem arbitriumque ejus honoris penes senatum fuisse,: semper infra aliorum aestimationes se metiens,; ; : aestimatione rectā severus, deterius interpretantibus tristior habebatur,—
Poet., the worth or value of a thing: Quod me non movet aestimatione,.

la:verb:aestimo.html:
aestĭmo (arch. aestŭ-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
from aes, with the termination -tumo, which also appears in autumo; cf.: legitumus, finitumus, maritumus; later, legitimus, finitimus, maritimus; compare the Goth. aistjan, to estimate
.
To determine or estimate the extrinsic (money) value of a thing, to value, rate, appraise; constr. with gen. or abl. (v. of price, Zumpt. §§ 444 and 456): domum emit prope dimidio carius quam aestimabat,: frumentum III denariis,: aliquid tenuissime,: prata magno,: perfecit (Aratus) aestimandis possessionibus, ut, etc.,; hence, litem alicui or alicujus, to estimate the value of an object in question, and thus determine how much the convicted person shall pay, to estimate or assess the damages; cf. , and Beier ad ; l. l.—
Trop., to estimate the intrinsic (moral) worth of a thing, to weigh, value, hold, etc. (while existimare, as a consequence of aestimare, signifies to judge a thing in any way after estimating its value: ex pretio rei judicare; cf. Burm. ad ; Herz. ad ; Corte and Kritz ad ; Gronov. ad ; ; and aestimator).— Constr.
That which serves as a standard by which a thing is estimated with ex or the abl.: vulgus ex veritate pauca, ex opinione multa aestimant,: aliquem ex artificio comico,: cum in Aquitaniam pervenisset, quae pars, ex tertiā parte Galliae est aestimanda, etc.,i. e. is to be reckoned as a third part,: amicitias inimicitiasque non ex re, sed ex commodo,.—With simple abl.: virtutem annis,: aliquid vitā, to measure a thing by life, i. e. to hold it as dear as life, : nec Macedonas veteri famā, sed praesentibus viribus aestimandos,.—
The value attached to a thing in estimating it, in the gen. or abl. pretii (cf. I.); poet. also with acc. nihil: auctoritatem alicujus magni,: quod non minoris aestimamus quam quemlibet triumphum, : aliquid unius assis,: aliquid permagno,: non magno,; so : non nihilo aestimandum,: magno te aestimaturum,: magno aestimantibus se,. And with definite numerals which give the price-current for which a thing may be had; cf. Zumpt. § 456; Corte: denis in diem assibus animam et corpus aestimari,: emori nolo, sed me esse mortuum nihil aestimo,.—
Among the histt. with a rel. clause.: aestimantibus, quanta futuri spe tam magna tacuisset,: quantopere dilectus sit, facile est aestimare, (but in , the correct read. is existumabitis, Dietsch).

aes, aeris (often used in
plur. nom. and acc.; abl. aeribus, Cato ap. Paul. ex Müll., and ; gen. AERVM, ), n.
cf. Germ. Eisen = iron, Erz = copper; Goth. aiz = copper, gold; Angl.Sax. ar, Ær = ore, copper, brass; Eng. iron, ore; Lat. aurum; with the com. notion of brightness; cf. aurora, etc.
.
Any crude metal dug out of the earth, except gold and silver; esp.,
Aes Cyprium, whence cuprum, copper: scoria aeris, copper dross or scoria, : aeris flos,flowers of copper,: squama aeris,scales of copper,: aes fundere,: conflare et temperare,: India neque aes neque plumbum habet,: aurum et argentum et aes,.—
An alloy, for the most part of copper and tin, bronze (brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, was hardly known to the ancients. For their bronze coins the Greeks adhered to copper and tin till B.C. 400, after which they added lead. Silver is rare in Greek bronze coins. The Romans admitted lead into their bronze coins, but gradually reduced the quantity, and, under Calig., Nero, Vesp., and Domit., issued pure copper coins, and then reverted to the mixture of lead. In the bronze mirrors now existing, which are nearly all Etruscan, silver predominated to give a highly reflecting surface. The antique bronze had about 87 parts of copper to 13 of tin. An analysis of several objects has given the following centesimal parts: statua ex aere, : simulacrum ex aere factum,: valvas ex aere factitavere,.—Hence: ducere aliquem ex aere,to cast one's image in bronze,; and in the same sense poet.: ducere aera,: aes Corinthium,, §§ 5-8; v. Corinthius.—
Meton.
(Esp. in the poets.) For everything made or prepared from copper, bronze, etc. (statues, tables of laws, money), and (as the ancients had the art of hardening and tempering copper and bronze) weapons, armor, utensils of husbandry: aes sonit, franguntur hastae, the trumpet sounds, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 213 Vahl.): Et prior aeris erat quam ferri cognitus usus: Aere solum terrae tractabant, aereque belli Miscebant fluctus et vulnera vasta serebant, etc.,: quae ille in aes incidit, in quo populi jussa perpetuasque leges esse voluit,; cf. ; ; ; : aere (with the trumpet, horn) ciere viros, : non tuba directi, non aeris cornua flexi, (hence also rectum aes, the tuba, in contr. with the crooked buccina, ); a brazen prow, ; the brazen age, .—In plur.: aera, Cato ap. Paul. ex Müll.; ; —
Money: the first Roman money consisted of small rude masses of copper, called aes rude, ; afterwards as coined: aes signatum,; ; so aes alone: si aes habent, dant mercem,: ancilla aere suo empta,: aes circumforaneum. borrowed from the brokers in the forum, : Hic meret aera liber Sosiis, earns them money,

345: gravis aere dextra,: effusum est aes tuum,: neque in zona aes (tollerent),: etiam aureos nummos aes dicimus,.—Hence,

Aes alienum, lit. the money of another; hence, in reference to him who has it, the sum owed, a debt, : habere aes alienum,: aes alienum amicorum suscipere,to take upon one's self,: contrahere,to run up,: facere,: conflare,; : in aes alienum incidere,to fall into debt,: in aere alieno esse,to be in debt,; so, aere alieno oppressum esse,; so : laborare ex aere alieno,: liberare se aere alieno,to get quit of,; so, aes alienum dissolvere,: aere alieno exire,to get out of,.—
In aere meo est, trop., he is, as it were, among my effects, he is my friend (only in the language of common conversation): in animo habui te in aere meo esse propter Lamiae nostri conjunctionem,; .—*
Alicujus aeris esse, to be of some value, .—*
In aere suo censeri, to be esteemed according to its own worth, .—
Sometimes = as, the unit of the standard of money (cf. as); hence, aes grave, the old heary money (as weighed, not counted out): denis milibus aeris gravis reos condemnavit,: indicibus dena milia aeris gravis, quae tum divitiae habebantur, data,; so, aes alone and in the gen. sing., instead of assium: aeris miliens, triciens,a hundred millions, three millions,: qui milibus aeris quinquaginta census fuisset,.—Also for coins that are smaller than an as (quadrans, triens, etc.): nec pueri credunt, nisi qui nondum aere, i. e. quadrante, lavantur (those who bathed paid each a quadrans), (cf.: dum tu quadrante lavatum Rex ibis,).—
Wages, pay.
A soldier's pay = stipendium: negabant danda esse aera militibus,. And soon after: annua aera habes: annuam operam ede.— Hence in plur., = stipendia, .—
Reward, payment, in gen., : nullum in bonis numero, quod ad aes exit, that has in view or aims at pay, reward, .—
In plur.: aera, counters; hence also the items of a computed sum (for which, later, a sing. form aera, ae (q. v.), came into use): si aera singula probāsti, summam, quae ex his confecta sit, non probare? Cic. ap. .

la:noun:aedilis.html:
aedīlis, is, m. (abl. aedili, ; ; ;
but aedile is more usual, P.; ; ; ; ; ; cf. Schne; Koffm. s. v.) [aedes], an œdile, a magistrate in Rome who had the superintendence of public buildings and works, such as temples, theatres, baths, aqueducts, sewers, highways, etc.; also of private buildings, of markets, provisions, taverns, of weights and measures (to see that they were legal), of the expense of funerals, and other similar functions of police. The class. passages applying here are: ; Müll.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Fest. s. h. v. p. 12; cf. Manut. ad and 6.—Further, the aediles, esp. the curule Ædiles (two in number), were expected to exhibit public spectacles; and they often lavished the most exorbitant expenses upon them, in order to prepare their way toward higher offices, ; ; . They inspected the plays before exhibition in the theatres, and rewarded or punished the actors according to their deserts, ; id. Cist. ep. 3; for this purpose they were required by oath to decide impartially,.—It was the special duty of the aediles plebeii (of whom also there were two) to preserve the decrees of the Senate and people in the temple of Ceres, and in a later age in the public treasury, . The office of the aediles curules (so called from the sella curulis, the seat on which they sat for judgment (v. curulis), while the aediles plebeii sat only on benches, subsellia) was created A.U.C. 387, for the purpose of holding public exhibitions, , first from the patricians, but as early as the following year from the plebeians also, .— Julius Cæsar created also the office of the two aediles Cereales, who had the superintendence of the public granaries and other provisions,.—The free towns also had Ædiles, who were often their only magistrates, ; ; ; ; v. further in Smith's Dict. Antiq. and Niebuhr's Rom. Hist. 1, 689 and 690.!*? Plaut. uses the word once adject.: aediles ludi, œdilic sports, Poen. 5, 2, 52.

la:adj:aeternus.html:
aeternus, a, um, adj.
contr. from aeviternus, Müll., from aevum, with the termination -ternus as in sempiternus, hesternus
,
without beginning or end, eternal (sempiternus denotes what is perpetual, what exists as long as time endures, and keeps even pace with it; aeternus, the eternal, that which is raised above all time, and can be measured only by œons (αἰῶνες, indefinite periods); for Tempus est pars quaedam aeternitatis,. Thus the sublime thought, without beginning and end, is more vividly suggested by aeternus than by sempiternus, since the former has more direct reference to the long duration of the eternal, which has neither beginning nor end. Sempiternus is rather a mathematical, aeternus a metaphysical, designation of eternity, Doed. Syn. I. p. 3).
Lit.
Of the past and future, eternal: deus beatus et aeternus,: nihil quod ortum sit, aeternum esse potest,: O Pater, o hominum rerumque aeterna Potestas,: di semper fuerunt, nati numquam sunt, siquidem aeterni sunt futuri,: idem legis perpetuae et aeternae vim Jovem dicit esse,: nomen Domini Dei aeterni,; : aeternum tempus,: causae immutabiles eaeque aeternae,. —
Of the future, everlasting, endless, immortal: natura animi ... neque nata certe est et aeterna est,: virorum bonorum mentes divinae mihi atque aeternae videntur esse,: aeternam timuerunt noctem,: Quod semper movetur, aeternum est,: Quidquid est illud quod sentit ... caeleste et divinum ob eamque rem aeternum sit, necesse est,: ut habeam vitam aeternam,; ; : in sanguine testamenti aeterni,: tu Juppiter bonorum inimicos aeternis suppliciis vivos mortuosque mactabis,: ibunt in supplicium aeternum,:

aeternas poenas in morte timendumst, : mitti in ignem aeternum,.—

Of the past: ex aeterno tempore quaeque Nunc etiam superare necessest corpora rebus,from eternity,: motum animorum nullo a principio, sed ex aeterno tempore intellegi convenire,.—
Spec. of objects of nature, which the ancients regarded as stable and perpetual, everlasting, eternal: aeterna templa caeli, Poët. ap. Müll.: aeternam lampada mundi,: micant aeterni sidera mundi,: aeterna domus, i. e. caelum,: donec veniret desiderium collium aeternorum,the everlasting hills,; ; cf. .—
Meton., of indef. long time.
Of the future, lasting, enduring, everlasting, perpetual: aeterni parietes,: dehinc spero aeternam inter nos gratiam fore,: aeternus luctus,: dolor,: vulnus,; so : aerumna,: mala,: bellum,: dedecus,: imperium,; so : versūs,: ignis sacerdotis,: gloria,: laus,: memoria,: non dubitat Lentulum aeternis tenebris vinculisque mandare,.—Comic.: spero me ob hunc nuntium aeternum adepturum cibum,. Esp. of Rome: aeterna urbs,the Eternal City,; ; Cod. Th. 10, 16, 1; ; .—Comp.: nec est ulli ligno aeternior natura. : aeterniora mala,.—
Of the past, of yore, of old: ablue corpus alluvii aeternisque sordibus squalidum,.—
Adv. phrases.
in aeter-num.
Lit., forever, everlastingly: et vivat in aeternum,: hoc nomen mihi est in aeternum,: Dominus in aeternum permanet,: vivet in aeternum,: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum,: non habebit remissionem in aeternum,.—
Meton., of indef. long time, forever, always: urbs in aeternum condita,: leges in aeternum latae,: (proverbia) durant in aeternum,: delatores non in praesens tantum, sed in aeternum repressisti,: (famulos) possidebitis in aeternum,: (servus) serviet tibi usque in aeternum,: ut sceleris memoria maneat in aeternum,.—
aeternum.

Of what is continually repeated, constantly, again and again (as in colloq. Engl., everlastingly, eternally): glaebaque versis Aeternum frangenda bidentibus,: ingens janitor Aeternum latrans (of Cerberus),.—

contr. from aegrimonia; as to the suppressed g, cf. jumentum from jugum, Doed. Syn. IV. p. 420. Others explain aerumna (with Paul. ex Fest. s. v. aerumnula, p. 24 Müll.) orig. for a frame for carrying burdens upon the back; hence trop.

(Ann. v. 47 Vahl.); cf.: Ilia dia nepos, quas erumnas tetulisti, id. ap. P. (Ann. v. 56 ib.): quantis cum aerumnis exantlavi diem, id. ap. (Trag. v. 127 ib.): uno ut labore absolvat aerumnas duas (of the pains of parturition),: animus aequos optimum est aerumnae condimentum,; ; so,; ; : lapit cor cura, aerumna corpus conficit, Pac. ap. ; ; : aerumna gravescit,: quo pacto adversam aerumnam ferant,: maeror est aegritudo flebilis: aerumna aegritudo laboriosa: dolor aegritudo crucians,: Herculis aerumnas perpeti: sic enim majores nostri labores non fugiendos tristissimo tamen verbo aerumnas etiam in Deo nominaverunt,; cf. : mors est aerumnarum requies,; so : Luculli miles collecta viatica multis Aerumnis, ad assem Perdiderat, with much difficulty, * : multiplicabo aerumnas tuas,: in labore et aerumnā (fui),.—
In later Lat. for defeat (of an army), ; cf. !*? At a later period, also, ĕrumna was written with short e, Paulin. Petric. Vit. D. . Hence, Enn. ap. P. derives it from eruere (quod mentem eruat). Cf. Doed. Syn. IV. p. 420.

Lit.: vis hostilis cum istoc fecit meas opes aequabiles,has made my property equal to his,: par (sc. est jus), quod in omnes aequabile est,: praedae partitio,: in descriptione aequabili sumptus,, so et saep.: mixtura vitiorum atque virtutum,.—

In relation to morals, equitable, just, right; constr. with in and acc. or absol.: status rei publicae. non in omnes ordines civitatis aequabilis,: fidus Romanis, aequabilis in suos,: jus aequabile,that deals alike with all,: aequabilium legum conditor, Aur, Vict. .—Comp., .— Adv.: aequābĭlĭter, uniformly, equally, in like manner, ; ; ; et saep. —Comp., .—Sup. does not occur either in the adj. or adv.

la:noun:aestus.html:
aestus, ūs (archaic
gen. aesti, Rib.; rare form of nom. plur. aestuus). m.
kind. with aestas and Gr. αἴθω; v. aestas
, an undulating, boiling, waving, tossing; a waving, heaving, billowy motion.
Lit.
Of fire; hence, in gen., fire, glow, heat (orig. in relation to its flashing up; while fervor denotes a glowing, ardor a burning, and calor a warming heat; yet it was early used for warming heat; v. the following example): nam fretus ipse anni permiscet frigus et aestum,heat and cold are blended, (for which calor, ): multa aestu victa per agros,: exsuperant flammae, furit aestus ad auras,: caniculae,; so : labore et aestu languidus,.—In plur.: neque frigora neque aestus facile tolerabat,.—So of midday heat: aestibus at mediis umbrosam exquirere vallem, (cf. : ille cum aestuaret, umbram secutus est).—And of the heat of disease (of

wounds, fever, inflammation, etc.): ulceris aestus, Att. ap. : homines aegri cum aestu febrique jactantur,.—

The undulating, heaving motion of the sea, the swell, surge: fervet aestu pelagus, Pac. ap. ; hence, meton. for the sea in agitation, waves, billows: delphines aestum secabant,: furit aestus harenis,: aestus totos campos inundaverant,.—In Verg. once of the boiling up of water in a vessel: exsultant aestu latices, Aen. 7, 464.—
Esp., the periodical flux and reflux or ebb and flow of the sea, the tide (cf. ; : aestus maris accedere et reciprocare maxime mirum, pluribus quidem modis, sed causa in sole lunāque,); : quid de fretis aut de marinis aestibus dicam? quorum accessus et recessus (flow and ebb) lunae motu gubernantur, : crescens,: decedens,: recedens,: secundus, in our favor, ap. : adversus, against us, id. ap. .—

The passionate ferment or commotion of the mind, the fire, glow, ardor of any (even a good) passion (cf. aestuo, II. A.): et belli magnos commovit funditus aestus (genus humanum),has stirred up from their very bottom the waves of discord,: civilis belli aestus, (cf. ): repente te quasi quidam aestus ingenii tui procul a terrā abripuit atque in altum abstraxit,: hunc absorbuit aestus quidam gloriae,: stultorum regum et populorum continet aestus,: perstet et, ut pelagi, sic pectoris adjuvet aestum,the glow of love,.—
A vacillating, irresolute state of mind, doubt, uncertainty, hesitation, trouble, embarrassment, anxiely: qui tibi aestus, qui error, quae tenebrae,: vario fluctuat aestu,: amor magno irarum fluctuat aestu,; cf. : aestus curaeque graves,.—
In the Epicurean philos. lang. of Lucretius, the undulatory flow or stream of atoms, atomic efflux, as the cause of perception (cf. affluo, I.): Perpetuoque fluunt certis ab rebus odores, Frigus ut a fluviis, calor ab sole, aestus ab undis Aequoris, exesor moerorum litora propter, etc.,; and in , the magnetic fluid is several times designated by aestus lapidis.

la:other:Aesculapius.html:
Aescŭlāpĭus, i, m., = Ἀσκληπιός, acc. to fable,
the son of Apollo and the nymph Coronis, deified after his death on account of his great knowledge of medicine, ; He had a temple at Rome, on the island in the Tiber. Upon the kind of worship paid to him, and his attributes, v. Festus, p. 82. Huic gallinae immolabantur, The principal seat of his worship in Greece was Epidaurus. In his temple there was a magnificent statue of ivory and gold, the work of Thrasymedes, in which he was represented as a noble figure, resembling that of Zeus. He was seated on a throne, holding in one hand a staff, and with the other resting on the head of a dragon (serpent), and by his side lay a dog. There were also other representations, one even as beardless, very common at an earlier period, Müll. Archaeol. d. Kunst, S. 534 and 535. That pertains to or is made of copper, bronze, etc.: aerarium metallum,a copper-mine,; ; fornaces,smelting-furnaces,: fabrica,the preparation of copper, faber, a coppersmith, (also aerarius alone; v. below).—

(Sc. faber.) One who works in copper, etc., a coppersmith: in aerariorum officinis,: aerariorum marculi,; so .—
(Sc. civis.) A citizen of the lowest class, who paid only a poll-tax (aera pendebat), and had no right of voting. Other citizens, upon the commission of great crimes, were degraded by the censors into this class, and deprived of all previous dignities. (Cf. and 29; Drak. ad ; Smith's Dict. Antiq., and Nieb. Röm. Gesch. 2, 63 and 452.) Referre aliquem in aerarios,. eximere aliquem ex aerariis, ext.; : omnes, quos senatu moverunt, quibusque equos ademerunt (censores) aerarios fecerunt et tribu moverunt,—
aerārĭa, ae, f.
(Sc. fodina, like argentaria and ferraria, : auraria,) A mine: multis locis apud eos (sc. Aquitanos) aerariae structuraeque sunt, Herz. —
(Sc. officina.) A smelting or refining house, .—
(Sc. fornax.) A smelting-furnace, .—

Gracchus, cum largitiones maximas fecisset et effudisset aerarium,, ; .—In the time of the emperors the aerarium (public treasure) was distinguished from fiscus (the wealth of the emperor): bona Sejani ablata aerario, ut in fisco cogerentur,; , ; v. fiscus. In the treasury the public archives were kept: factum senatus consultum, ne decreta patrum ante diem decimum ad aerarium deferrentur,; cf. ; ; ; and also the standards: signa ex aerario prompta,.—The Quaestores aerarii (under Augustus and his immediate successors the Praetores) presided over the aerarium, with whom the Tribuni aerarii were associated as assistants; cf. Quaestor and Tribunus.—The aerarium contained also a fund, established after the invasion of Gaul, and augmented by the immense booty acquired in the wars with Carthage, Macedonia, Corinth, etc., as well as by the tribute of the manumissi, which could be used only in cases of extreme public necessity, hence with the epithet sanctius,: aurum vicesimarium, quod in sanctiore aerario ad ultimos casus servaretur, promi placuit,; cf. ; (of the Syracusans). Hence trop., : aerarium militare, destined by Aug. for defraying the expenses of war,; ; .
